title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
Let’s back up a bit
In the first week of the semester, we discussed rates. When cases become counts, counts become rates, and rates become something that can fairly be compared across areas with different populations. This is related to Assignment 4 and the input for most pattern analysis we will do afterwards: Moran’s I, cluster detection, and the Bayesian models all start from observed and expected counts.
Important reading: Moraga 5.2. We will be using the same Pennsylvania lung cancer data in the second part of this notebook.

library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(SpatialEpi)   # pennLC data; expected()

theme_set(theme_classic(base_size = 12))







Note



If SpatialEpi is missing, install.packages("SpatialEpi") once.

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
1.1 Why aggregate at all
Health data rarely arrive as the counts we map. They arrive as records: a diagnosis, a death certificate, an address. We (or epidemiologists) aggregate them to areas for three reasons. Denominators — the population at risk — exist only for areas, from the census. Confidentiality rules usually forbid releasing point locations. And most reporting (state registries, CDC WONDER) is area-based already.

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
section: 1.2 Aggregating points: a worked example from North Carolina
text:
1.2 Aggregating points: a worked example from North Carolina
Real case addresses are confidential, so in this example we fabricate them. We scatter a set of 667 SIDS deaths of 1974–78 at random inside their North Carolina counties, then pretend we received only the points.


Code
nc <- st_read(system.file("shape/nc.shp", package = "sf"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(32119)                           # NC State Plane, metres

set.seed(374)
cases <- st_sample(nc, size = nc$SID74) |>      # one point per death
  st_sf() |>
  mutate(case_id = row_number())

nrow(cases)


[1] 671


Aggregation is a point-in-polygon operation. Before running it, one check that saves more grief than any other:


Code
st_crs(cases) == st_crs(nc)                     # must be TRUE


[1] TRUE


(note: If the two layers are in different CRSs, sf will stop you — but only if both CRSs are declared. A shapefile with a missing .prj fails silently).

1.2.1 Counting points in polygons
st_intersects() returns, for each county, the points inside it; lengths() counts them. Counties with no cases get a zero.


Code
nc$n_cases <- lengths(st_intersects(nc, cases))

sum(nc$n_cases)                                 # should equal nrow(cases)


[1] 671

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
1.3 Counts are not risk


Code
p1 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = nc, fill = "grey95", colour = "grey70", linewidth = 0.2) +
  geom_sf(data = cases, size = 0.4, colour = "#b2182b") +
  labs(title = "Cases (synthetic locations)")

p2 <- ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = n_cases), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Reds", direction = 1, name = "Cases") +
  labs(title = "Counts")

p3 <- ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = BIR74), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Greys", direction = 1, name = "Births") +
  labs(title = "Births")

p1 / p2 / p3 & theme_void(base_size = 12)








Figure 1: Case locations, county counts, and births. The counts mostly redraw the population.





The count map is mostly a population map: Mecklenburg, Wake, and Guilford have many deaths because they have many births. A count needs a denominator before it says anything about risk — which is where the rest of today begins.

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
section: 1.4 From counts to a crude rate
text:
1.4 From counts to a crude rate
Dividing each county’s count by its births gives the crude SIDS rate:
\[
\text{crude}_i = \frac{O_i}{\text{births}_i} \times 1{,}000
\]


Code
nc <- nc |>
  mutate(crude = 1000 * n_cases / BIR74)        # per 1,000 births

1000 * sum(nc$n_cases) / sum(nc$BIR74)          # statewide rate


[1] 2.033568


Code
ggplot(nc) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = crude), colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_distiller(palette = "Reds", direction = 1, name = "Per 1,000\nbirths") +
  theme_void(base_size = 12)








Figure 2: Crude SIDS rate per 1,000 live births, North Carolina 1974–78.





The picture changes: the large urban counties no longer dominate. The highest rates are in small counties such as Anson (15 deaths among 1,570 births, 9.6 per 1,000) and Northampton, against a statewide rate of about 2.0. Rates built on so few births are unstable. —

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
2.1 Three measures, three questions
Incidence counts new cases arising in a population over a period of time. Prevalence counts existing cases at a point (or short window) in time (~cross-section, snapshot). Mortality counts deaths, and is an incidence measure whose event is death. For surveillance and aetiology we usually want incidence; prevalence mixes incidence with duration, so a disease that lasts longer looks more common even if it arises no more often.
Incidence itself comes in two forms, and the distinction matters for the denominator.









Measure
Numerator
Denominator
Units




Cumulative incidence (risk)
new cases in period
population at risk at start
proportion, over a stated period


Incidence rate
new cases in period

proportion

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
2.2 Person-time
The incidence rate divides by the total time individuals spent at risk. Ten thousand people followed for five years contribute roughly 50,000 person-years; 50 new cases gives a rate of 1 per 1,000 person-years. For area data we never observe individual follow-up, so person-time is approximated as
\[
\text{person-years}_i \approx \text{mid-period population}_i \times \text{years in period}.
\]
For a single calendar year, the mid-year population is the person-time approximation, which is why annual registry rates are expressed “per 100,000 population”.






WarningRead the denominator before the number



The NC SIDS rate is deaths per 1,000 live births — a proportion of a birth cohort, not a rate per person-year. The 1974–78 and 1979–84 periods are five and six years long, yet their rates per 1,000 births are comparable because births, not years, are the denominator. Divide deaths by BIR74 * 5 and you have produced a number with no clear meaning.

The crude rate ignores strata: all cases over all people.
\[
\text{crude}_i = \frac{O_i}{P_i} \times 100{,}000
\]


Code
county <- d |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarise(
    O    = sum(cases),                                         # observed
    pop  = sum(population),
    p60  = sum(population[age %in% c("60.69", "70+")]) / pop,  # share aged 60+
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(crude = 1e5 * O / pop)

pa_rate <- 1e5 * sum(county$O) / sum(county$pop)               # statewide
pa_rate

ggplot(pa_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(crude, quantile(crude, 0:5 / 5), include.lowest = TRUE)),
          colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "YlOrRd", name = "Per 100,000") +   # sequential
  theme_void()

section: 3.2 What the crude rate is really measuring

3.2 What the crude rate is really measuring
Lung cancer risk rises steeply with age. The stratum-specific rates show how steeply:


Code
d |>
  group_by(age) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), pop = sum(population)) |>
  mutate(rate_per_100k = round(1e5 * cases / pop, 1))

A county whose residents are older will therefore have a higher crude rate even if every age group in it faces exactly the statewide risk. The crude rate is a weighted average of the stratum-specific rates, and the weights are the county’s own age structure.


Code
ggplot(county, aes(p60, crude)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = pop), alpha = 0.5, colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "grey30", linewidth = 0.6) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(x = "Population aged 60+", y = "Crude rate per 100,000", size = "Population")








Figure 4: Crude rates partly track age structure.





The association is modest (r ≈ 0.3) — smoking and other exposures vary too — but it is enough to reorder counties, as we will see. Comparing crude rates thus confounds risk with demography. Standardization removes that confounding; here we use the indirect method, which gives the SMR.

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
4.1 Expected counts
Ask how many cases each county would have had if every stratum in it experienced the statewide risk. Apply the reference rates \(r_j\) to the local population \(n_{ij}\):
\[
E_i = \sum_j r_j\, n_{ij}, \qquad r_j = \frac{\sum_i O_{ij}}{\sum_i n_{ij}} .
\]
Only the reference rates need to be stable, and they are computed from the whole state. Each county contributes nothing but its population counts.


Code
ref <- d |>
  group_by(race, gender, age) |>
  summarise(r_ref = sum(cases) / sum(population), .groups = "drop")  # 16 rates

E_tbl <- d |>
  left_join(ref, by = c("race", "gender", "age")) |>
  group_by(county) |>
  summarise(E = sum(population * r_ref))


SpatialEpi::expected() does the same thing, as in Moraga 5.2. It assumes the rows are sorted by area and then by strata in the same order within every area; nothing checks this for you.


Code
d_sorted <- d |> arrange(county, race, gender, age)

E_se <- expected(
  population = d_sorted$population,
  cases      = d_sorted$cases,
  n.strata   = 16
)

all.equal(E_tbl$E, E_se)                        # identical


[1] TRUE


Because the reference rates come from these same data (internal standardization), expected counts sum to observed counts:


Code
c(observed = sum(county$O), expected = sum(E_tbl$E))


observed expected 
   10279    10279

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
4.2 The SIR (and the SMR)
\[
\text{SIR}_i = \frac{O_i}{E_i}
\]
An SIR of 1 means the county had as many cases as its demography predicts; 1.2 means 20% more; 0.8 means 20% fewer. For deaths the same ratio is called the SMR. The indirectly standardized rate puts it back on the rate scale: \(\text{SIR}_i \times\) the reference crude rate.


Code
county <- county |>
  left_join(E_tbl, by = "county") |>
  mutate(
    SIR   = O / E,
    lower = qchisq(0.025, 2 * O) / (2 * E),          # exact Poisson 95% CI
    upper = qchisq(0.975, 2 * (O + 1)) / (2 * E)
  )

summary(county$SIR)


   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.3203  0.8251  0.9555  0.9316  1.0590  1.3747

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
4.3 Mapping the SIR
An SIR has a natural midpoint at 1, so a diverging palette is defensible here (unlike most rates — recall Week 1). Breaks are symmetric on the ratio scale.


Code
pa_map <- pa |> left_join(county, by = "county")

sir_breaks <- c(0, 0.67, 0.83, 0.95, 1.05, 1.2, 1.5, Inf)

ggplot(pa_map) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = cut(SIR, sir_breaks)), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "RdBu", direction = -1, drop = FALSE, name = "SIR") +
  theme_void()








Figure 5: Raw SIRs for lung cancer, Pennsylvania 2002, standardized by race, sex, and age.

title: Aggregated Data and Incidence Rates
text:
5.1 Precision is not uniform


Code
ggplot(county, aes(SIR, reorder(county, E))) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_linerange(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(size = E), colour = "#b2182b") +
  labs(x = "SIR (95% CI)", y = NULL, size = "Expected") +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 6))








Figure 7: SIRs with exact 95% intervals, ordered by expected count.





Forest, Cameron, and Sullivan each expect fewer than ten cases; their SIRs span most of the map’s colour range and their intervals span nearly all of the plausible range. Philadelphia and Allegheny expect over a thousand. The map colours them with the same confidence. That is Tuesday’s problem.






NoteIf you use spdep::probmap()



It returns expected counts and a relative risk, but relRisk is scaled by 100: a county at the reference level has relRisk = 100, not 1. Divide by 100 before comparing it with an SIR, or thresholds such as “SIR > 1.2” will flag nearly every county.
